title: Ari Vesalainen väittelee aiheesta Mallien toiminta, arviointi ja tutkimuksellinen riski tekstien tunnistusjärjestelmissä
content:
M.Sc. Ari Vesalainen defends his PhD thesis “Model Behavior, Evaluation, and Scholarly Risk in Historical Text Recognition Systems” on Thursday the 22nd of October 2026 at 13 in the University of Helsinki Metsätalo Building, Room B317 (Hall 6, Unioninkatu 40, 3rd floor). His opponent is Professor Antoine Doucet (University of La Rochelle, France) and custos Professor Laura Ruotsalainen (University of Helsinki). The defence will be held in English.

The thesis of Ari Vesalainen is a part of research done in the Spatiotemporal Data Analysis group in the Department of Computer Science and in the Computational History group in the Department of Digital Humanities at the University of Helsinki. His supervisors have been Professor Laura Ruotsalainen and Professor Mikko Tolonen (University of Helsinki).

title: Palkittu geenitutkimus selvitti long Covid -oireyhtymän riskitekijöitä
content:
Some people experience persistent symptoms for months or even years after a coronavirus infection. This condition is known as long COVID. Common symptoms include debilitating fatigue, brain fog and respiratory problems.

One of the key findings of the award-winning study was that genetic susceptibility to long COVID is linked to the regulation of lung function. In particular, the FOXP4 gene emerged as an important factor, helping researchers better understand the cellular mechanisms underlying long COVID.

The study was led by Hanna M. Ollila, a group leader at the Institute for Molecular Medicine Finland (FIMM), University of Helsinki.

The interdisciplinary study analysed genetic data from more than one million people across 16 countries. In Finland, the researchers used data from FinnGen, which includes more than half a million biobank participants.

According to Ollila, the findings highlight the importance of FinnGen and other population-based studies in understanding chronic conditions that develop following infections.

title: Melioristikahvila kokoontuu marraskuussa ensimmäistä kertaa
content:
The first Meliorist café on November 4, 2026 at 15–16 invites the audience to discuss the current state of Finnish child protection services with psychiatric nurse (HUS) Tuitu Tynjälä. What does the increasing hopelessness of young people tell us? Can our current services answer the need and suffering that young people encounter? The event is in Finnish.

Meliorist café is organized by the Centre of Excellence in Meliorist Philosophy of Suffering. It discusses suffering in the contexts where we encounter it: in our everyday lives, in the society, and globally. How is suffering visible in our lives? How do we talk about it and what stance do we take on it? What can we do about suffering and how can we ameliorate it?

The next Meliorist café takes place on January 19, 2027 at 15–16.

title: Anwar Arifin’s Weavers of the Distant Past, Part 1
content:
Anwar Arifin is a doctoral researcher in economic anthropology. As a member of the WORK-IT project, he is currently researching about the historiography of the Ancient Near East, and what kind of assumptions are born from modern social, political, and economic theory that influence the way scholars perceive and produce the history of the Ancient Near East.

How did you end up researching the topic of your book?

I joined the group a bit later than the others. My first idea was to approach the project by tracing the histories of two disciplines: economics and the social sciences, and Ancient Near Eastern studies. At first, I had accepted the conventional view that these were two separate things. Looking into their histories quickly made that assumption hard to sustain.

Turns out the progenitors of these disciplines participated in the same debates about language. Since I'm trained as an anthropologist, I do ethnography as well, and one thing I always notice is that it comes down to a problem of language.

title: Saijaliisa Kangasjärvi tutkii kasvien stressiä
content:
In my research group, we focus on two main themes. First, we study how plants respond to light stress and adapt to changing light conditions. Second, we investigate interactions between plants and pathogens, as well as the defence mechanisms plants use. 

Many plant defence compounds influence the appearance, taste and health benefits of vegetables, making these compounds particularly significant. We apply what we learn through basic research to indoor vegetable cultivation and efforts to extend the shelf life of fresh produce.

I hold a joint professorship in translational plant biology at the Faculty of Biological and Environmental Sciences and the Faculty of Agriculture and Forestry.

Our work has advanced understanding of how plant stress biology can be applied to improve sustainable indoor cultivation and the quality of produce after harvest. We have collaborated with companies and fellow researchers through national and international research networks and joint projects. 

For example, we have contributed our expertise in plant biology to studies of fresh, ready-to-eat salad mixes.

title: Luonnontieteellisen museon Elämän historia -sali sulkeutuu tammikuussa – uusi näyttely avautuu loppuvuodesta 2028
content:
The Natural History Museum’s History of Life is one of the museum’s most popular exhibitions. However, the exhibition, completed in 2008, has long been in need of an update, as it is outdated both in terms of content and exhibition technology.

– The new exhibition will present evolution and the development of biodiversity in a more spectacular and tangible way than before. This is the museum’s most significant renewal project in years, says Sanna Vuori, Head of the Public Engagement Unit at the Finnish Museum of Natural History.

The dinosaurs Giganotosaurus carolinii and Shunosaurus lii in the History of Life exhibition have become familiar to many museum visitors over the years. They will remain in the new exhibition but will be joined by never-before-seen reconstructions of prehistoric animals. Among other things, a reconstruction of the otter-like early whale Ambulocetus natans is currently being built in the museum’s conservation facilities.

title: Southnord Artfest 2026: Roots En Route
content:
Roots En Route is a multi-sensory installation by four artists who will create a multi-sensory installation in dialogue with the greenhouses – examining rootedness and displacement; asking what grows where it was planted and what survives the crossing. The African plants that fill the greenhouses carry their own histories of movement and adaptation.

Camille Norment in collaboration with Sofia Jernberg create a soundscape drawing on the insects and birds of the plants' homelands. Toubab Holmes' site-specific scent installation traces the hidden journeys of plants through the extractive system of perfumery. Charmaine Watkiss visits the botanical legacies and healing traditions of her Caribbean ancestry through large-scale drawings of Plant Warriors. Together, the three works read the botanical garden as an archive of movement, and the plants in it as things that were carried, taken and made to travel.

Running from October 2026 through January 2027, the exhibition offers a long, unhurried encounter between art and the plant world. Set aside more time than you think you need. Walk slowly, sense carefully, and let yourself be immersed.

title: “Ilman pölyttäjiä maailma olisi ankea ja väritön” – Uusi näyttely avaa oven pölyttäjien kiehtovaan elämään
content:
Pollinators represent an astonishingly diverse group of animals, many of which possess remarkable abilities despite their small size. Bees can count, bumblebees solve problems, and on distant islands, even lizards can pollinate flowers.

The  exhibition, which combines science and art, offers a wealth of information, stunning visuals, and fun activities for visitors of all ages. Guests can play interactive games like "Identify the Pollinators" and "Pollinator Protection Bingo," design their own imaginary pollinator, and explore the museum's impressive collection of specimens. The exhibition is based on a newly illustrated non-fiction book.

– We want to show the world through the eyes of pollinators, says exhibition scriptwriter Mia Rönkä, Adjunct Professor in Environmental Ecology at the University of Turku. Rönkä has written the exhibition’s informational texts and poems.

Although the sensory perceptions, cognitive abilities, and communication methods of pollinators like bees differ from ours as humans, we can still strive to understand and appreciate them as individuals of other species – without anthropomorphizing them, Rönkä explains.

title: Ukrainan sota - yliopiston suositukset
content:
The University of Helsinki has condemned the military action by Russia and expressed its support for Ukraine and its university community. We have also expressed our support for Ukraine, together with other Finnish universities, through statements by and the . As a demonstration of support, we have illuminated buildings in the colours of the Ukrainian flag and raised the flag on our premises.

One of the principles of the University of Helsinki is to promote international collaboration in research and higher education, and to support these efforts even in difficult circumstances. Russia’s indefensible military aggression in Ukraine has required exceptional measures, which include those taken in the collaboration between universities.

The University of Helsinki is monitoring both national and EU-level sanctions, adapting our policies and processes accordingly. Together with other Finnish and international universities, the University of Helsinki strives to promote the end of military action in Ukraine, while supporting Ukrainian institutions and people.

title: Sairaalafyysikko on sädehoidon, diagnostiikan ja leikkaussalien näkymätön asiantuntija
content:
The RAPTOR (Resuscitation with Angiography, Percutaneous Techniques, and Operative Repair) suite in the Meilahti Tower Hospital is an impressive synthesis of operating theatre and imaging laboratory. Dedicated to the emergency treatment of trauma patients, the room is not only equipped for surgical operations, but also for imaging patients on the operating table without the need to move them, thanks to a sliding gantry CT scanner. The room also has devices for performing ultrasonographies and angiographies, the latter being used specifically to check blood vessels.

Because imaging produces radiation, a shielding structure is located next to the operating table. This shield can protect as many as 18 people when imaging is ongoing.

“We spent a long time designing it so that moving back and forth between the shield and the table could be done as quickly as possible,” explains Professor of Medical Physics of the University of Helsinki. He was involved in designing the RAPTOR suite together with other medical physicists in Meilahti.

title: LekaMed continues – Focus on democratic education, participation and agency
content:
How can adults and children together create a more democratic everyday environment in early childhood education and pre-primary education? is one of the questions explored during the project this autumn. Throughout the autumn, Marina and Sara are working closely with a pre-primary education group and its staff to explore this and related questions. 

Alongside the collection of research data, staff are supported in their professional development in matters related to democratic education, participation, and agency. Material developed in collaboration with Petra Holm at Moilo is being tested together with staff in the group, while different approaches to creating a more democracy-promoting everyday environment are also being explored. 

Through this collaboration, we aim to develop approaches and practices that can be shared with other professionals working in early childhood education. The goal is to contribute to a culture in which children can experience democracy and where children’s voices are given genuine space and taken seriously, says Marina.
